papers.title: General-purpose moment tensor potential for Ga–In liquid alloys towards large-scale molecular dynamics with ab initio accuracy
papers.abstract: Abstract Liquid metals demonstrate significant potential for applications in thermal management and flexible electronic circuits, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of their transport properties for technological advancements. Experimental measurement of these properties presents challenges due to factors like cost, corrosion and impurity control. Consequently, accurate computational simulations become essential for predicting the physical properties of these materials. In this research, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to model several properties of gallium (Ga), indium (In) and Ga–In alloys, including lattice structural parameters, radial distribution functions (RDF), structure factors, self-diffusion coefficients and viscosity. Due to the difficulty of traditional interatomic potentials in capturing the short-range interactions directly related to the mechanical behavior of liquid atoms, machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have been constructed to precisely describe the liquid metals Ga, In, and Ga–In alloys. This was achieved by utilizing the moment tensor potential (MTP) framework in combination with an active learning strategy. MTP was trained using a comprehensive database generated from DFT and MD simulations, which include a variety of crystal structures, point defects and liquid structures. The calculations of physical properties in this research have shown strong consistency with experimental data, demonstrating that the MTP can accurately describe the interatomic interactions between Ga–Ga, In–In and Ga–In. Our work has established a novel paradigm for investigating the physical properties of various liquid metal systems, offering valuable insights and references for future research.

papers.title: Analysing the Intersection of Education and Data Science: Enhancing Learning Outcomes through Information Systems -An Analytical Study
papers.abstract: The current research will investigate the relationship between education and data science, concerning information systems in an attempt to establish how learning can be enhanced. In other words, current data trends in educational sectors can help optimize the existing approaches to learning processes, address students' needs, and stimulate their interest and motivation. The study focuses on how information systems can be used in capturing, processing, and using education information for purposes of decision-making. These systems make it possible for teachers to track students' performance in real-time, analyze the students' learning profile, and even forecast their performance shortly hence designing instructions befitting the students. It also explores different fields of data science including passive and active learning, predictive analysis, and data mining to analyze their effectiveness in improving curriculum and assessment approaches and other learning processes. Furthermore, the research examines the difficulties of implementing data science in education frameworks; data protection and technology, and the training of teachers and faculty, among them. Based on a review of the literature and analysis of empirical literature, this paper establishes best practices for the implementation of information systems in education. Consequently, the areas of data science highlighted here indicate that the positive outcomes in terms of effective organizational resource management, increase in students' retention and increased learning performance are possible if the data science is applied correctly. Additionally, the study highlights the need for integration of technology-based solutions with learning objectives, in ways that technological solutions do not supplant conventional pedagogical practices but supplement them. The study provides a list of recommendations to policymakers, educators, and educational technologists about how data science and Information systems can be utilized for designing and developing adaptive student-cantered learning contexts. The study adds to the existing literature on the application of data science in education and provides valuable implementable strategies to enhance learning in the current emerging technology and result-driven academic environment.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Enhancing Panic Disorder Detection using Ensemble and Resampling Techniques
papers.abstract: Panic disorder is one of the leading mental health problems that entail serials of extreme fear that can highly hinder an individual's activities of daily life. Sometimes, intervention is very important, understanding the problem is highly crucial. Unfortunately, some methods assist with diagnostics do not provide accuracy in identification. Using machine learning approaches can resolve this problem as accuracy can be improved with data-driven models. This paper used ensemble machine learning models, Random Forest, Bagging Classifier, and Balanced Bagging Classifier to identify panic disorder. Medical datasets usually have a class imbalance problem. Therefore, we performed resampling SMOTE, ADASYN, and Tomek Links. We evaluated these models by accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC AUC, Cohen's Kappa, uncertainty measures, aleatoric uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, and predictive entropy. In our results, The Bagging Classifier was out performance with the highest accuracy (99.97%), recall (99.66%), F1-score (99.60%), and Cohen’s Kappa (99.58%), minimal uncertainty metrics (aleatoric: 0.00062, entropy: 0.002003), establishing itself as the optimal model for panic disorder diagnosis. This study proves the effectiveness of ensemble learning and resampling methods for early panic disorder diagnosis and future mental health technologies.

The implementation of an AI animation tool was assessed using user engagement metrics and thematic analysis of feedback from both students and teachers. Initial classroom trials indicated a 25% increase in student participation when AI animations were integrated into lessons, compared to traditional teaching methods. Furthermore, 80% of students reported that the AI-based animations made learning more enjoyable and accessible, citing improved understanding and sustained interest in classroom activities. The findings highlight the effectiveness of AI-based animations in fostering active learning and engagement. This approach supports the Merdeka Curriculum’s principles of autonomy, collaboration, and adaptive pedagogy. By catering to diverse student needs and promoting a more dynamic classroom environment, AI-driven tools offer promising pathways for future educational innovation.

To supplement the loss of accuracy and reliability in the proposed model, the controller introduces a moving horizon estimator to observe the unmeasured state variables under the poor communication condition of a low-voltage distribution network. papers.title: Boundary-Based Active Domain Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation Under Adverse Conditions
papers.abstract: Existing domain adaptation semantic segmentation (DASS) methods under adverse conditions often depend on pseudo-labels for network training. However, these pseudo-labels are frequently plagued by noise and bias toward high-confidence predictions, thereby impeding the enhancement of segmentation performance. This article tackles the above challenge by proposing a novel boundary-based active domain adaptation (ADA) framework, which efficiently selects both informative low-confidence samples and high-confident but misclassified samples to be labeled while maximizing the segmentation performance under a limited annotation budget. For the evaluation of sample confidence and informativeness, we first propose ranking weighted feature space impurity (RWFSI) metric to quantify category distribution among a sample's nearest neighbors within the feature space and consider the samples with higher RWFSI values as low-confidence samples around the decision boundary, which can also alleviate the category imbalance of active labels. Subsequently, we apply Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to model the distribution across source and target domains. Using the spatial arrangement of each GMM component, we define the intraclass domain shift score (ICDSS), which identifies samples with high ICDSS values as those more likely to be high-confidence but misclassified, aiding in refining sample selection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method is superior to the existing state-of-the-art domain adaptation and active learning (AL) methods and comparable with those of full supervision. The code will be released at https://github.com/1061018609/BADA.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Decline of Critical Thinking: A Hidden Academic Crisis in Contemporary Education Systems
papers.abstract: This study investigated the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on students’ critical thinking, cognitive engagement, and strategies for balancing AI integration in contemporary education systems. A quantitative research design was employed, with a sample of 230 undergraduate and graduate students selected through convenience sampling from diverse academic disciplines. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, multiple regression, and ANOVA tests. These findings showed that there was strong negative correlation between AI use and critical thinking (r = -0.482, p < 0.01), which suggests that overuse of AI tools can reduce critical thinking and reflective thinking. A further analysis of the results using multiple regression analysis showed that the use of AI had a negative effect on the engagement (b = -0.401, p < 0.001), whereas independent learning had a positive effect on engagement (b = 0.332, p < 0.001). The outcomes of the ANOVA analysis revealed that the strategies with the combination of AI and the active learning, inquiry-based, and problem-solving techniques were found to be much more effective at promoting the critical thinking process compared to the purely automated ones (F = 34.12, p < 0.001). papers.title: Design and Validation of a Volumetric-extrusion Bioprinter for Bioprinting of Soluble Basement Membrane Extract for Translational Research
papers.abstract: In translational research, 3D in vitro models are essential for advancing scientific understanding and therapeutic development. To this aim, Soluble Basement Membrane Extracts (SBMes), derived from mouse sarcoma cells, play the key role of replicating mechanical and biochemical features of in vivo microenvironment. They are particularly valuable in a variety of research fields, from tissue engineering to drug testing. In particular, they have become fundamental in cancer research as traditional 2D cell cultures, widely used in the field, can provide misleading information since they do not capture the three-dimensional (3D) structure and tumor microenvironment. In cancer research, effective 3D in vitro models are crucial for better understanding cancer evolution and anticipating challenges, such as drug resistance mechanisms. Organoids have emerged as promising 3D in vitro models, offering a more accurate representation of tumor biology. They grow in SBMes as they create an environment where cells can grow and self-organize into 3D structures. However, SBMe presents significant challenges, including low mechanical properties and complex rheological behavior, preventing its use with commercially available pneumatic-extrusion bioprinting systems. To address these limitations, we developed a low-cost, volumetric-controlled bioprinting system and a specific protocol for printing structures with SBMe. This system is based on a volumetric extruder and overcomes the limitations of traditional pneumatic-driven approaches. Once assembled and programmed with a specific g-code, the system can bioprint both pure and diluted SBMe to obtain both single and multi-layer constructs. This approach offers a more reliable and scalable method for producing 3D cell culture models, paving the way for more effective research into novel treatments and drug testing.

papers.title: Construction and application of a novel 3D bioprinting-based in vitro nasopharyngeal carcinoma model for drug screening and mechanistic research
papers.abstract: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a prominent head and neck malignancy, yet the mechanisms underlying its occurrence, progression, recurrence, metastasis, drug resistance, and radiation resistance have not been fully understood. This knowledge gap is partly due to the lack of preclinical NPC models for research. Compared to traditional 2D cell cultures, 3D bioprinting (3DP) offers significant advantages in replicating the tumor microenvironment. However, no studies to date have used 3DP technology to model NPC. In this study, we used extrusion-based 3DP to develop a new preclinical NPC model (3DP-HK1) using the emerging bio-ink gelatin methacryloyl. The model successfully demonstrated the ability to sustain long-term tumor cell activity. Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence analyses demonstrated that 3DP-HK1 largely retained the histopathological features and tumor-related protein expression of NPC. In addition, we conducted a wound healing experiment, which indicated that tumor cells in 3DP-HK1 have stronger migration ability than 2D-cultured cells (2D-HK1), highlighting differences in cellular phenotype. The different responses of 3DP-HK1 and 2D-HK1 to various anti-tumor drugs and radiation reflect the advantages of 3DP-HK1 for preclinical drug screening and exploring mechanisms of radiotherapy in NPC. Transcriptome sequencing revealed that 3DP-HK1 has a distinct gene expression profile compared to 2D-HK1, with significantly upregulated expression of malignant genes, such as keratin 6B (KRT6B), S100 calcium-binding protein A8 (S100A8), and crystallin alpha B (CRYAB). Meanwhile, genes associated with drug resistance (e.g., lysine demethylase 5B [KDM5B]) and radiation resistance (e.g., carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A [CPT1A]) were also upregulated, confirming findings from other experimental analyses at the RNA level. In conclusion, this study successfully constructed a 3DP-based preclinical model for NPC research and proved its reliability and significant potential for advancing drug screening and mechanistic studies.

papers.abstract: Perhaps you’ve heard of the “Choosing Wisely” campaign by the American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) Foundation, which sought to “spark conversations between clinicians and patients about what tests, treatments, and procedures are needed—and which ones are not” [3]. If you haven’t heard of it, I’m sorry to bring you some bad news. After an 11-year run, the ABIM Foundation no longer maintains its list of treatments that physicians should walk (or run) away from. Or, to borrow a phrase from my Millennial friends, I'm actually “sorry, not sorry,” since the call of Choosing Wisely to our specialty was so faint you might not have heard its whisper. Likewise, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) has recommended we avoid a list of interventions we’ve long since quit performing, medications and supplements that we don’t typically recommend, and treatments we don’t get paid to use [6]. The “expanded” AAOS list from 2020 [1] suggested we stop “routinely performing arthroscopy with lavage and/or debridement in patients with a primary diagnosis of symptomatic osteoarthritis of the knee” (hot on the heels of a “discovery” published in NEJM nearly 20 years earlier [8]), that we avoid unselectively using continuous passive motion machines after knee replacement, and that we quit routinely prescribing opioids to patients with knee osteoarthritis, hip osteoarthritis, low back pain, or rotator cuff injury. The pediatric orthopaedic version of this was similarly unimpactful [2], recommending, among other things, that we shun screening hip ultrasounds to rule out developmental hip dysplasia in babies who have no risk factors and normal hip exams and that we not recommend x-rays, bracing, or surgery for children under the age of 8 who have “mild in-toeing”—news that was old when the earth was young (that is, when I was a resident). I suppose we shouldn’t be too surprised that fellow-driven organizations are shy about recommending against interventions their fellows get paid to perform. Unfortunately, the list of low-value interventions in our practices is long; by some definitions, it is longer than the list of “necessary services,” according to one healthcare analytics firm [7], and placebo-controlled surgical trials suggest that many of our go-to procedures may not be as good as we believe they are [4, 5]. It's clear enough that good data aren’t changing our practices very quickly. So perhaps it’s better if we pivot to anecdote. Narrative may touch our hearts more gently than do data, and touching hearts may be the best way to change minds. I was especially moved by this opener to an essay on the topic: “Let me say at the outset that in my primary care clinic I practice low-value care. Not every day, but often enough. Probably every week. For example, when patients show up with a list of tests that [the surgeon says need] to be done before they can get their cataracts fixed, I do them. I want them to be able to see [10]”. I honor the author of that for saying the quiet part out loud. We’re all in her boat to some degree. Sometimes we really do have to cut against the evidence to take care of our patients. Interestingly, and in the example I’m covering in this month’s Editor’s Spotlight/Take 5 article [9], we may sometimes have to ignore the evidence to take care of ourselves. The article in question by Atul F. Kamath’s group from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, OH, USA found little evidence in favor of a step that adds cost to the millions of total hip and total knee arthroplasties that are performed each year—the use of surgical helmet systems associated with body-exhaust suits—but still offered some rationale for why that step might still be worth taking [9]. The best available evidence in their systematic review found that surgical helmet systems in total joint arthroplasty increase the level of contamination of sterile fields in the operating room environment, on other surfaces (like surgical attire), and in operating room air. Though the sources for these findings were mainly experimental studies that counted bacterial colonies, they found scant evidence that using these helmet systems helps prevent infections, and I’m not aware of any robust evidence on this topic. They do note, though, that surgical helmet systems seem effective as personal protective equipment for surgeons, and because many surgeons see them that way, Dr. Kamath’s team made some sensible suggestions for how to don the gear so as to minimize contamination [9]. Though most readers don’t perform hip and knee arthroplasty, we all can think of examples in our practices where best evidence comes into tension with common practice, so facing that tension directly seems important. Join me in the Take 5 interview that follows, as Dr. Kamath does just that. Most of our conversation is about the big picture on these important topics, and isn't so much about arthroplasty stuff; for that reason, I think this interview will be of interest to all orthopaedic surgeons. Take 5 Interview with Atul F. Kamath MD, senior author of “Is Your Surgical Helmet System Compromising the Sterile Field? A Systematic Review of Contamination Risks and Preventive Measures in Joint Arthroplasty” [9] Seth S. Leopold MD:Congratulations on this somewhat troubling article [9]. Let’s leave aside the arthroplasty-related implications for a few minutes and focus on the big picture. Normally, the burden falls on those who think we should adopt (or continue to use) some tool or technology to prove to us why we ought to do so, particularly if it comes at a cost. Yet so many unproven or ineffective treatments and tools persist in the absence of that proof. Why is this such a problem in our specialty?Atul F. Kamath MDAtul F. Kamath MD: The issue of unproven or ineffective treatments in our specialty is considerable and persistent. In this world of rapid innovation, there's often pressure to adopt “innovative” technologies quickly, sometimes before their true clinical value has been established. This issue extends beyond tools and technologies to include orthopaedic procedures and implants, where robust, high-quality evidence often is lacking before widespread adoption. The case of metal-on-metal hip implants serves as a sobering reminder—these were initially marketed as more durable alternatives, but specific implants were later found to have serious complications like metallosis and high failure rates. Unfortunately, by the time these issues became apparent, thousands of patients had already received these implants. The problem persists because of a complex interplay of factors. Marketing is perhaps the most obvious—device manufacturers invest heavily in promoting their products, which can obscure the lack of evidence for their efficacy. These marketing campaigns create both physician and patient expectations for new, better, “cutting-edge” technologies, often in the absence of robust clinical data to support their use. When “new technologies” are associated with “superior care”—as is the case in the minds of so many patients today—surgeons feel pressure to adopt the latest innovations to stay competitive. This cycle perpetuates the use of technologies that may not demonstrably improve patient outcomes in the short term. The reality is that much of what we do in medicine is based on experience, anecdote, training bias, and individualized preferences. For instance, surgical helmet systems were introduced with the promise of reducing prosthetic joint infection rates. While the original “Charnley-style” suits—along with an almost fanatical approach to aseptic surgery—made a dent in infection rates, this finding generally hasn't held for many or most helmet and body suit systems since then. It may be troubling but not unfounded that our study [9] and those of others [11-13] have questioned the dogma that these devices result in infection mitigation in modern-day arthroplasty. All of this highlights the critical need for high-quality research—like randomized controlled trials and comprehensive registry data—to properly evaluate the short- and long-term effectiveness of the novel technologies and interventions we bring to patients. Orthopaedic surgery is a hotbed of learning, creativity, and applied science; there's an undeniable appeal of novel tools and technologies within our field. But without an evidence-based approach, we risk not only unnecessary healthcare expenditures, but, more importantly, potentially compromised patient safety and outcomes. Dr. Leopold:Your paper identified what I think a big—though not the only—cause of that problem is: the idea that for some topics, we actually will never be able to get the definitive answer with any confidence from randomized trials. The underlying event of interest in your paper is prosthetic joint infection, but none of the studies you included could actually address that issue head-on because the event rate is too low to compare interventions in well-designed trials. Where else in orthopaedic research does this problem—that of serious or lethal events that are also rare—come up, and how should practicing surgeons deal with the fact we may never get high-quality evidence to justify our decisions? Dr. Kamath: Medicine is fraught with these rare, adverse events. In addition to prosthetic joint infection, other rare but serious complications that have been particularly challenging to study include life-threatening thromboembolic events after a variety of orthopaedic procedures (including but not limited to total joint arthroplasty), issues initially deemed to be subclinical but would end up being catastrophic implant failures, and “silent” osteolysis leading to revision surgery, to name a few. Adverse events like pulmonary embolism are rare but carry a real risk of death. It is daunting to think about the costs and complexities that will be required to orchestrate studies that are large enough to answer these questions. The infrequency of these rare yet serious events presents a real challenge to conducting large-scale randomized controlled trials, often leaving clinicians to navigate these waters with a mix of available data, clinical experience, and consensus-based guidelines. National/multicenter registries—such as the American Joint Replacement Registry, European registries, and the Australian/New Zealand Joint Registry—will play an increasingly instrumental role in allowing us to collect and analyze data (and hopefully patient-level data) on rare implant events. Data from these registries have been crucial in understanding trends in revision rates and complications due to their ability to provide a larger sample size than any single study could achieve. When confronting these rare but potentially devastating complications, registry data and well-designed systematic reviews and meta-analyses provide valuable insights, even if they don't always offer definitive answers. It’s important that we be candid with our patients about the limitations of our evidence base while using surrogate endpoints judiciously to help inform our decision-making. Looking ahead, continued collaboration across institutions remains crucial for building our understanding of these significant but uncommon events. While perfect evidence may remain elusive for some of these complications, our collective experience and careful documentation of outcomes can help guide clinical practice. Other forums, like the International Consensus Meeting, blend systematic review of the available evidence with expert opinions from and debates among international delegates, including me. Dr. Leopold:Surrogate endpoints can be so difficult to interpret. In your paper [9], the surrogate endpoints were things like colony counts, which don’t easily translate to clinical events. We will never know, for example, how big a difference in colony counts is big enough to result in an increased PJI risk, and just looking for “any difference” is certainly too sensitive, if an intervention takes time, money, or itself carries risk. This plays itself out in many other areas—how much of a difference in pullout strength of a suture anchor would matter in a biomechanical study, how much micromotion in a fusion construct is enough to care about—and I always struggle with papers that traffic in these things. How do you read them as a busy clinician? Dr. Kamath: I agree that drawing conclusions from papers with surrogate endpoints is often challenging. In such instances—when the results don't directly have a clinical translation—I start by critically evaluating how well the surrogate reflects actual, important clinical outcomes, and then consider the implications of those outcomes. If an outcome is one with significant implications, such as prosthetic joint infection, I'm more likely to consider adjusting my practice to err on the side of caution, despite having imperfect data. Cost is always a key consideration in my mind, as well—for interventions that demand considerable resources, I need to see really strong data to consider implementation. I find it particularly helpful when studies with surrogate endpoints provide context about the practical implications of their findings. For example, a study demonstrating reduced contamination with a specific intervention should also discuss its feasibility, cost, and alignment with clinical practice. A thorough discussion of the limitations or challenges in interpretation of these endpoints is fruitful. This contextualization helps bridge the gap between laboratory findings and clinical decision-making. In biomechanical studies, like those examining pullout strength or micromotion, I look for authors to relate their findings to known clinical failure modes or established mechanical thresholds that have been correlated with clinical outcomes. Ultimately, as clinicians, we must balance the pursuit of perfection with pragmatic decision-making. We must balance our hunger for innovation and better patient outcomes with the realities and limitations of our science. While surrogate endpoints may not provide absolute answers, they can guide us in refining our techniques and protocols when interpreted within the broader context of clinical experience and patient care priorities. The key is to maintain a critical yet practical perspective, always considering how the findings might translate to meaningful improvements in patient outcomes. Dr. Leopold:What would it take for our specialty to arrive at a more impactful campaign along the lines of “Choosing Wisely”? By that, I mean some kind of a list of commonly used but low-value (or harmful) surgical procedures that would gain sufficient traction to bend surgical usage curves downward? Dr. Kamath: That's really a great, thought-provoking question. First, we’d need consensus among experts to identify practices with low value or potential harm. For instance, routine use of knee arthroscopy for degenerative joint disease has been scrutinized for its limited benefit in most patients. Clinical guidelines and evidence-based recommendations from organizations like the AAOS can serve as a foundation for identifying these practices, gauging the evidence, and incorporating multiple stakeholders into the guideline outputs. However, identifying low-value procedures is just the beginning. The real challenge lies in changing established practice patterns. This requires widespread education and engagement of both surgeons and patients. Surgeons need to understand not just what practices to avoid, but why—that is, the evidence (or lack thereof) in support of specific, common procedures and interventions that we perform. Patients need to be active participants in these discussions, understanding both the traditional and alternative treatment options available to them. We as medical professionals are also in constant dialogue with insurance companies regarding evidence to support payments for certain procedures—a hot topic at this time. What will ultimately drive change is data. We're trained to follow the numbers, so when institutions that adopt these guidelines demonstrate tangible benefits—whether through improved patient outcomes, reduced complications, or cost savings—others will follow suit. Success stories from respected institutions can create a domino effect, particularly if they're willing to share their implementation strategies and results. While this transformation won't happen overnight, the potential impact on patient care and healthcare resource utilization makes it worth pursuing. Dr. Leopold:At last, one for the arthroplasty surgeons who are still reading: In your study [9], you identify one reason for this specific technology to persist in the absence of benefits to patients in terms of infection prevention, which is the idea that surgical helmet systems may help surgeons protect themselves from bloodborne exposures. It seems obvious to me (as an arthroplasty surgeon) that they do offer a benefit in that regard. But I’ll say two things about that: (1) We don’t know how much of a benefit it offers in that regard, and (2) your study suggests that it may come at a cost to our patients in terms of infection risk. How can or should we balance these seemingly competing values? Dr. Kamath: Balancing these competing priorities requires a nuanced and evidence-based approach. Our study highlighted a paradox: While surgical helmet systems may protect surgeons from bloodborne exposures, they may not reduce infection rates in patients, and if improperly used, they might inadvertently increase contamination risks because of disrupted laminar airflow or the movement of particles in the sterile field. This creates a challenging tension between surgeon safety and patient outcomes. Orthopaedic surgeons are at high risk for aerosolized and direct pathogen exposures, which can cause life-threatening disease. papers.title: Effect of Pore Size on Mechanical Properties of Ti-6Al-4V Metal Foams
papers.abstract: Bulk Ti-6Al-4V is used for biomedical applications, such as prosthetic hip and knee joints due to some momentous characteristics, i.e., excellent strength to weight ratio, corrosion resistance and moderate Young’s modulus. The objective of the study was to investigate the effect of varying pore size on the mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4V metallic foam. NaCl was used in order to introduce porosity within the matrix. Final sintered products had porosity in the range of 62 % to 74 %. Compressive strength and Young’s modulus of sintered pellets were found to be in the range of 23 MPa to 3 MPa and 2 GPa to 0.84 GPa, respectively. In this research fabricated metal foams have comparable mechanical properties to that of cancellous bones.
